title: TurboFlex
status: Launched April 2026 (U.S. and Canada); Miami-Dade approval in progress
description:
TurboFlex was my last and largest program at CRL: a dry-glazed glass railing system brought from OnLevel in Europe to the U.S. and Canadian markets under the CRL name, in about six months from first gate to launch.

A glass railing is a guard. It keeps people from falling off balconies, terraces and mezzanines, so every part of it answers to building codes, structural engineers and certification bodies before it can be sold. The system had been engineered and tested to German DIN standards; my job was to prove it under U.S. codes, put it through Miami-Dade's hurricane impact testing, set up a three-country supply chain, and get product, packaging, pricing and training ready for 23 service centers on a fixed launch date.

It replaced CRL's Taper-Loc system, which had been losing share for three years. TurboFlex cuts the parts an installer has to stock from 178 to 10, swaps a large, expensive installation tool for a torque-limited bit that runs on a standard drill, and adds height adjustment on top of tilt, which the market was starting to expect.

brief.label: Problem
brief.text: CRL's Taper-Loc dry-glaze system had been largely unchanged for over 12 years. Competitors offered lower entry cost, more adjustment and wider glass compatibility, and some large Miami installers wouldn't carry it without High-Velocity Hurricane Zone approval. Sales fell 17.5% from 2022 to 2024.

brief.label: Strategy
brief.text: Bring in a proven European system as CRL's premium dry-set railing and keep Taper-Loc as the entry-level option, so existing customers aren't stranded and new ones enter through TurboFlex.

brief.label: Solution
brief.text: One base shoe in two mounts (top and fascia), three clamp sizes that cover the common glass range, 2° of tilt plus height adjustment, and a torque-limited install bit in place of a dedicated tool.

brief.label: Customers
brief.text: Architects, glass temperers, and large and small glazing contractors on commercial and high-end residential projects.

brief.label: Market
brief.text: Glass railing systems: about $2.8B worldwide in 2022, projected to reach $4.9B by 2030 (7.7% CAGR).

brief.label: Competition
brief.text: FHC Achieve, Q-Railing, Wagner and VIVA Railings.

my_role:
I led the program day to day, from the business case at Gate 0 through launch, alongside the senior product manager for the category. I ran the gate reviews, the weekly cadence with marketing, sourcing and leadership, a daily stand-up with the engineering team, and a bi-weekly call with OnLevel's leadership in Europe.

Because a railing is life-safety equipment, the work was as much about evidence as product. I coordinated the engineering report that translated OnLevel's German test results into U.S. load requirements, the update to CRL's ICC-ES evaluation report, the Miami-Dade test samples and approval package, and the supplier quality controls that approval requires. In parallel I built the forecast and inventory plan, set pricing with revenue operations, created the SKUs and drove the packaging, labeling, freight and training plans that put the system in 23 service centers.

recovery_title: Plan to win back the dry-glaze market
recovery_intro: Taper-Loc wasn't failing on quality. It was losing on entry cost, stocking complexity, adjustment and Florida certification. The plan addressed each one rather than discounting the old system.

recovery.label: Lower the cost of entry
recovery.text: A torque-limited bit that runs on the drill installers already carry replaces a large, expensive dedicated tool, the most common complaint we heard.

recovery.label: Make it stockable
recovery.text: Three clamps and one base shoe cover the glass range that used to take 178 parts, so installers can keep inventory on the truck and quote jobs faster.

recovery.label: Win back Florida
recovery.text: Miami-Dade HVHZ impact testing passed at 75 psf for both mounts, the certification large Miami installers named as their reason for buying elsewhere.

recovery.label: Transition without stranding customers
recovery.text: Taper-Loc stays as the entry-level system while its inventory runs down, supported by a promotion on its install tool; TurboFlex brings in new customers as the premium tier.

recovery.label: Ramp deliberately
recovery.text: The plan assumes slow adoption, typical of railings: 20% of former dry-set volume in year one, rising to 80% by 2030, with a domestic extruder to cut tariff exposure.

challenges.challenge: The system was engineered to German DIN standards. U.S. codes load a guard differently, and certification bodies needed U.S. evidence before we could sell it as a life-safety product.
challenges.resolution: I commissioned an independent engineering report that translated the DIN test results into U.S. load requirements and anchorage tables for steel, concrete and wood. In parallel, the clamp kits were re-tuned for U.S. glass thicknesses and tolerances, and the system was added to CRL's ICC-ES evaluation report.

challenges.challenge: Miami-Dade testing needed custom base shoes sized to the test chamber, short enough to air-freight. The supplier had no undrilled stock, so the samples would have waited until late January while the test plan went back and forth on anchor spacing.
challenges.resolution: I made the anchor-spacing call with engineering to stop the loop, specified pre-drilled 91" shoes, and air-freighted them with clamp kits and torque tools. The system passed impact testing at 75 psf in both top and fascia mount.

challenges.challenge: Miami-Dade grants product approval to manufacturers, and a third-party-built system needs documented controls at the factory, not only at our dock.
challenges.resolution: We built the county's quality expectations into the supplier plan: audit rights, incoming-material and mill-certificate traceability, compliant labeling, and third-party inspection, so the approval would hold up after launch as well as at submission.

challenges.challenge: Packaging, labels, barcodes and the in-box instructions all had to be finished across three companies and two holiday shutdowns, and CRL's barcode standard changed in the middle of the process.
challenges.resolution: I connected OnLevel directly with our marketing, inventory-control and brand teams, consolidated open items into one list with owners, and caught a mismatch between the clamp count shown in the instructions and the kit before it went to print. Labels moved to the sides of the boxes so they read on stacked pallets, and the second order's packaging was redesigned around the installer's workflow, fitting 24 more boxes per pallet.

challenges.challenge: A strong pre-launch at GlassBuild pushed demand well past the original forecast, and leadership asked for a second order before the first had landed.
challenges.resolution: I re-planned quantities SKU by SKU with sourcing and demand planning, set up the new cladding, end-cap and custom parts in SAP, and the second order was confirmed in March, doubling the first.

challenges.challenge: Inventory, 125 displays and samples had to reach 23 service centers before training, and the freight forwarder, buyers and supplier were each working from different partial information, including a currency mismatch between the purchase order and the contract.
challenges.resolution: I consolidated pickup, packing and pallet data into one thread, split shipments between air and sea by priority, and held invoicing to the contract terms leadership had agreed so goods weren't held up. Training for inside sales, branch managers and outside sales ran April 6 to 8, and the system launched April 15.

challenges.challenge: A 50% tariff on imported aluminum squeezed launch margins on the base shoe.
challenges.resolution: We launched on imported stock to hold the date, priced TurboFlex as the premium tier, and started qualifying a U.S. extruder so long-term the only imported parts are the clamp kits.
